Fifa has been approached for comment.
More to follow.

articles.headline: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts to miss rest of season after blood clots travel to his lungs
keyFacts: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will miss the rest of the season after testing revealed blood clots in his lungs, the team announced.
The team stated that Hurts is in stable condition with a good prognosis and is expected to make a full recovery.
Hurts will be treated with blood thinners and cannot participate in contact activities until he is off the medication.
body: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will miss the rest of the season after further testing revealed blood clots in his lungs, the team announced Monday.

Hurts’s condition is considered stable and he “has no significant functional limitations,” the team said. His treatment for a new diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli will involve blood thinners, during which time he is unable to participate in contact activities.
The 28-year-old’s prognosis is good and the team said it expects a full recovery with no long-term effects.

Specialists in London initially diagnosed superficial clots in Hurts’ left calf after Philadelphia’s 19-17 loss against the Jacksonville Jaguars on 11 October. Further testing discovered multiple blood clots in his lungs.

“We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners,” the team’s statement concluded. “In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects.”

Hurts hadn’t missed more than two games in a season since becoming the Eagles’ full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago.

Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the Eagles’ 25-14 loss to Carolina. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020.

Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle of a five-year, $255m extension, including $179.3m guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season.

The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in the NFL.

articles.headline: Japanese acting union fights back against AI-generated voice use, proposing strict new guidelines, especially regarding the use of a deceased actor's voice
keyFacts: The Japan Actors Union introduced new guidelines and restrictions to protect voice actors from generative AI exploitation.
The rules require explicit consent, compensation for AI replications, protection of translated performances, and a ban on using deceased actors' voices without prior lifetime authorization.
The union plans to push the Japanese government to pass binding laws protecting voice rights, though the current guidelines are not legally binding.
body: The Japan Actors Union has issued new rules, guidelines, and restrictions related to AI-generated voice use. This includes an outright ban on the replication of the voices of dead actors, unless the actor had authorised its use during their lifetime.

Per Automaton, these guidelines are meant to protect an industry that has been exposed to exploitation by generative AI. One example includes voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda (Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man) taking Tiktok to court in an attempt to remove AI-generated voice imitations from the platform. He would go on to lose that case, but not without setting a precedent that a person's voice is subject to protection under publicity rights laws.

The guidelines cover four major points. The first is focused on consent and establishes that permission must be granted at "every stage" of the generative AI process. This would mean AI companies require permission from actors before models are trained on their performances.

The second point, meanwhile, states that AI replications of an actor's work are to be counted as a new performance under the guidelines. This would mean royalties or compensation must be paid by AI companies to the actors involved.

Next up comes generative AI-powered translations, which takes an actor's performance and automatically changes it to another language. These must maintain the "artistic integrity" of the original performance, the guidelines state, and may not be used without permission in overseas regions.

Lastly, the Japan Actors Union covers generative AI use regarding a dead actor's work. The union's guidelines ban the use of generative AI here, unless that actor had given express permission for the software's use while they were alive. Even with this, an AI company would require permission from the deceased actor's family, the agency or company the actor was affiliated with, and to pay royalties.

"The Japan Actors Union will strive to not just establish these guidelines as industry-wide rules, but also strengthen its efforts to encourage the government to legislate regulations that protect 'voice rights'," wrote The Japan Actors Union (translated by Automaton). "Technological advancements will not stop, but the 'living, breathing human expression' and a 'respect for rights' must always remain at its core."

It is worth noting that these guidelines are not laws and therefore are not binding rules AI companies must follow. Even so, it marks a major push from the Japan Actors Union for this to change. These new guidelines contribute to mounting pressure against the generative AI industry in Japan, as actors continue to push for better protections.

Japan's Voice Actor Union is not the only one pushing back against generative AI. In Western countries, similar collectives have been speaking out about the technologies' impact on the field, with one describing it as "catastrophic".

articles.headline: GameSir Nova Lite 2 review
keyFacts: The GameSir Nova Lite 2 is a wireless budget controller for PC priced at $30 or £30.
It features Hall effect sticks, a mechanical D-pad, trigger stops, and programmable rear buttons.
Reviewers noted drawbacks including a lack of grip, small shoulder buttons, and basic software.
body: Our Verdict
A new benchmark for budget gamepads, the GameSir Nova Lite 2 has a tremendous feature set for something that costs as much as a couple of overpriced coffees.
For
- Very affordable
- Hall effect sticks
- Wireless (2.4 + Bluetooth)
- Mechanical D-pad
- Trigger stops
Against
- Not much grip
- Shoulder buttons are a little small
- Basic software
PC Gamer's got your back
Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

The GameSir Nova Lite 2 is our new best budget controller for PC. It's extremely well equipped considering the small asking price. Depart with just $30/£30 of your hard-earned cash, and you'll receive a wireless controller with Hall effect sticks, mechanical D-pad, trigger stops, and programmable rear buttons.

There's enough here that even GameSir's own exceedingly popular G7 Pro is at risk of cannibalisation. The Nova Lite 2 doesn't look that out of shape by comparison, with only quality of life and more advanced features between them. Such as a handful of micro switches and a bigger battery. The G7 Pro is a better all-round controller, but for less than half the cash, the Nova Lite 2 is tough to ignore.

There are some drawbacks with a controller at this price. The plastic doesn't feel great and it's not overly grippy. The software could be smarter and the shoulder buttons wider, too. But they all seem savvy sacrifices for the savings that the Nova Lite 2 delivers.
Buy if...

✅ You don't use a controller often and you're not looking to spend a lot of money: If you use a mouse and keyboard for most of your gaming, you don't need the next best thing. A dependable, wireless pad like the Nova Lite 2 is plenty sufficient for the odd singleplayer game.
Do not buy if...

❌ You want lots of customisation: You can't change the thumbsticks out on the Nova Lite 2, nor are the trigger stops switching between different types of actuation as with more high-end pads. There's no lighting, only a couple of extra buttons, and the software could be better. But, hey, not everyone is into that sorta thing.
A new benchmark for budget gamepads, the GameSir Nova Lite 2 has a tremendous feature set for something that costs as much as a couple of overpriced coffees.
GameSir Nova Lite 2 - Features
The Nova Lite 2 is less than half the price of the G7 Pro, but it's not at a loss for many of the same or similar features. This budget gamepad really packs a lot in.

First off, it offers wireless connectivity at a low cost. It supports 2.4 GHz for PC, via a USB Type-A dongle, and Bluetooth for Android, iOS and Switch. Using the 2.4 GHz dongle, I measured a range exceeding 20 metres, in line of sight, so I wouldn't worry about range at any sensible distances (though Bluetooth and a wall or two will notably trim that down).

Then there are the Hall effect sticks. These sorts of sticks are becoming pretty ubiquitous among gamepads these days—that or TMR, as found in the G7 Pro 8K—but they lower the chance of pesky stick drift making an appearance later in life. This pair lack the premium feel of more expensive controllers but they're otherwise pretty great.

The triggers are also Hall effect, though most are, and offer two modes: full range of movement or stubby li'l clicks. You might get some use out of the shortened trigger stops in fighting games—a more tactile controller may be better suited—though they do come in handy when using the Nova Lite 2 with a Switch 2. I've been using the Lite 2 on Switch and it's very well suited for a mean Mario Kart machine like myself.
The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The mechanical D-pad is a standout feature. It has a great, lightweight click in each direction. It doesn't take much to actuate but you can be quite deliberate with it. For more casual users, it's great for clicking through menu screens, though it could just as reliably be mashed repeatedly in a fighting game.

The face buttons are standard fare. They're just membrane and aren't anything special. The two rear buttons are also not particularly tactile, being hewn from the same plastic as the housing on the controller. That, too, is just okay. I don't expect much more from a controller at this price tag, but it doesn't feel like it's going to break apart between your hands, either. There's no major flex to any of the plastic housing and only a little creakiness when pressed firmly.

Now, for one thing I don't actually like about this controller, and that's the plastic travel case that comes with it. I get the idea, and hey, if you travel with your controller often, it saves the thumbsticks, but for many people, myself included, it feels a bit like plastic waste I could've done without.
GameSir Nova Lite 2 - Value

The Nova Lite 2 is superb value for money at $30/£30. It lacks some more advanced features, such as a gyro, but makes more than up for it with practical, real-world benefits, such as a mechanical D-pad and Hall effect thumbsticks.

It's a step up over the existing Nova Lite. That's on its way out as our pick as the best budget controller, to be replaced by the Nova Lite 2. That controller is still an option for a slightly reduced fee of $23/£18, but the Nova Lite 2's rear buttons, trigger stops, and mechanical D-pad wholly justify the slight increase in cost for me.
Considering the cost of some wired controllers these days, the wireless Nova Lite 2 feels like a bit of a steal.
GameSir Nova Lite 2 - Ergonomics

The Nova Lite 2 is very, very normal. It's slightly less sculpted than a modern Xbox pad, but has a similar shape. The rear plastic is ever so slightly textured, adding the tiniest amount more grip. Most buttons are easy to reach without moving my hands much, including the extra rear buttons. The only real oddity is how small the bumpers are: they don't extend around the corners of the controller like most pads these days.

It comes in black or white. Both have orange highlights around the thumbsticks, orange switches on the rear triggers, and orange legends on the face buttons. Big Stadia Controller vibes—remember Stadia?
I'm really scraping the bottom of the barrel for things to describe here. This thing is plain, but not offensively so.
GameSir Nova Lite 2 - Software
GameSir Connect is the best way to control the Nova Lite 2 on PC. It's a bit basic as far as modern software goes, though the core functionality one might expect is all in there.

You can control the deadzone for each of the thumbsticks and triggers, vibration intensity, rear button assignments, and lighting within the app. There's just one bonus feature: hair trigger mode. This is loosely equivalent to rapid trigger on some modern gaming keyboards, in that the trigger will click and release based on the relative movement of the trigger, not its absolute position. As GameSir says in the app, it's "useful for scenarios that need fast triggering."
The GameSir Connect app also offers software updates for the controller. Best use it at least once.

There's also a mobile application, simply called GameSir, but it has just two out of five stars on the App Store and a weaker UI than the desktop app. I'd not bother unless you're strictly mobile/Switch only.
Finally, there are ways to configure the controller without any software whatsoever. I appreciate this option for the software-averse among us—even if the actual combos are tough to remember.

So, selecting between PC (X + GameSir) and Bluetooth (B + GameSir) is easy enough, but remapping the back buttons (M + L4/L5, followed by the key to remap), turning on Turbo mode (M + any button), and turning on hair trigger mode (M + LT/RT) might require the manual for a reminder.
GameSir Nova Lite 2 - Gallery
GameSir Nova Lite 2 - Battery life

GameSir doesn't note a specific battery life for the Nova Lite 2. It simply offers a battery capacity, which sits at 600 mAh. That's the same as the Nova Lite, which had a stated 10-hour battery life, so we can more or less assume a similar expected result for the Nova Lite 2.

I've measured how long it takes for the controller to go from 100% to 0% over the course of a couple of gaming sessions. It took roughly eight and a half hours. I suspect with the lighting disabled and a different style of play, it'd be possible to crack the expected 10-hour mark, but either way, it lasts long enough to not cause an issue.
A new benchmark for budget gamepads, the GameSir Nova Lite 2 has a tremendous feature set for something that costs as much as a couple of overpriced coffees.

Jacob has been writing about PC hardware and technology for over eight years. He earned his first byline at PCGamesN before joining PC Gamer. He spends most of his time building PCs, running benchmarks, and trying his best to learn Linux.

articles.headline: Majority of Americans think Donald Trump is using presidency to enrich himself, new poll finds – live
keyFacts: New polling shows a majority of Americans think Trump is using presidency to enrich himself, including a third of Republicans A new Washington Post-ABC poll shows that Donald Trump’s approval rating has reached a new low – 33%.
This comes, just over two weeks away from the November midterms, as the president continues crisscrossing the country as part of his campaign blitz for embattled Republicans.

body: New polling shows a majority of Americans think Trump is using presidency to enrich himself, including a third of Republicans
A new Washington Post-ABC poll shows that Donald Trump’s approval rating has reached a new low – 33%.
This comes, just over two weeks away from the November midterms, as the president continues crisscrossing the country as part of his campaign blitz for embattled Republicans.

Notably, the new polling also shows that a majority (66%) of Americans believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. Looking at that data even further – 34% of Republicans believe Trump is enriching himself. This is a 12-point jump from last September.
Today’s new polling suggests Americans remain deeply pessimistic about the economy ahead of the midterms, with 75% rating conditions as either “not so good” or “poor.”
The findings also highlight the challenge facing Republicans in November: 37% of respondents said they trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 28% who said they trust Republicans.

This comes as Trump continues his midterms campaign blitz this week. He’ll head to Kansas on Monday to stump on behalf of embattled GOP incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, before back-to-back events in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan.

Today’s announcement comes as billions of dollars have been scrapped from NIH research budgets. Almost 8,000 grants have been cancelled at the institute and the US National Science Foundation alone, and more than 1,000 NIH employees have been fired since Trump returned to office in 2025.
Earlier this year, my colleague Ed Pilkington, reported on the brain drain that was affecting the key agency that conducts biomedical and public health research.

A quick note that Donald Trump’s executive order signing at 11am ET will be to create a new Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House Women’s Health taskforce, according to a White House official.
A reminder that Melania Trump, the first lady, will also be at the event.

The boss of a New York-based sticker company, whose staunch support for Donald Trump prompted him to record a Maga-themed rap album and call for an extension of Mount Rushmore to add the president’s face, is running for Congress.
Anthony Constantino, who began a brief pro boxing career at age 40, is the Republican candidate for GOP congresswoman Elise Stefanik’s seat in New York’s 21st district.

While Trump won the district by 21 points in 2024, and it has been represented by a Republican in the US House of Representatives since 2015, the party’s lead appears to have dwindled significantly as Constantino, 43, campaigns for voters to send him to Washington.

His lead in recent polls has fallen to single digits; one survey earlier this month put him four points behind. In September, the Cook Partisan Voting Index shifted the race from solid Republican to likely Republican. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the district to its Red to Blue program in early October.

“I’m running for Congress. I built a company with over 1,000 people. Not an easy thing to do,” Constantino said, referring to his company, Sticker Mule. “I went pro in boxing at the age of 40. Not an easy thing to do.”
Mike Tyson “decided to endorse me”, he added in an interview, claiming the former boxing world champion had only endorsed four candidates. “It’s not easy to get endorsed by Mike Tyson.”

Most political candidates lay out their agenda in lengthy publications, or campaign speeches. In December 2025, Constantino released a 20-track album – titled Thank You President Trump – which praised the president’s alleged golfing prowess and described how the world purportedly loves him. It took two weeks to complete, according to a press release.

“I just realize it’s good to be different, first of all,” Constantino said of the album. “Secondly, some people like listening to speeches. Other people like listening to music. Not everybody in this country wants to listen to political speeches.”

Also on Truth Social today, Donald Trump has repeated his baseless claims that the riots sweeping France – which initially began as protests against deteriorating school infrastructure and an overstretched education system – are due to mass migration.
“The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” Trump wrote on social media.
A reminder that French authorities have not linked the riots to immigrants.

Over the weekend, hundreds of thousands demonstrated throughout the country. However, chaos erupted at a number of protests, which saw buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested.
French president Emmanuel Macron and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, have blamed the violence on “factious” ultra-leftwing groups.
Within the new polling from the Washington Post and ABC, 48% of respondents said they are financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025.
According to the Post, that represents the highest percentage saying this about any president in this series of polls since 1986.

A majority of those surveyed – 67% – also said that Trump is not committed to protecting freedom of the press. This comes after a protracted battle to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House grounds. A federal judge has subsequently issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration from enforcing the ban.
Meanwhile, 61 % people also said that Trump is not committed to free and fair elections, according to the poll.

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington. We’ll hear from him, and the first lady, Melania Trump, when they sign an executive order in the Rose Garden at 11am ET.

The president will then travel to Wichita, Kansas, where he’ll hold a midterms rally at 7pm ET to stump for Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, who we noted earlier is facing a increasingly competitive re-election race against his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton.
Hamilton, a pastor, is hoping to be the first Democratic senator that Kansans send to Washington in almost a century.
We’ll bring you the latest as that gets under way.
US disaster survivors still await at least $10bn in federal aid: ‘It’s devastating’

Survivors of extreme weather disasters across the US are facing long waits for government assistance funds to rebuild their lives, with the last long-term recovery funds allocated for Hurricane Milton that hit Florida two years ago. Government officials estimate more than $10bn is needed in long-term disaster recovery funding to rebuild affected communities in Los Angeles county and St Louis, Missouri, alone.

Since 1993, more than $111bn have been appropriated and allocated for CDBG-DR. But the long-term recovery program has no standing fund, meaning that Congress must appropriate the money disaster-by-disaster. This has caused long lag times in recovery funding before. Survivors of the 2020 earthquakes in Puerto Rico waited 655 days after the disaster was declared for CDBG-DR funding to be allocated, according to a Bipartisan Policy Center report.

In July 2026, CDBG-DR was written into law for the first time, authorizing the program for three years. While advocates hoped the legislation would create a reliable framework to disseminate disaster relief funds more quickly, no more money has been appropriated for the CDBG-DR program.
US ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.

Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupied West Bank towns.

The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
Huckabee, a rightwing ally of Donald Trump with a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine.

“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”
Trump brands federal judge who slowed his golf project a ‘crazed lunatic'
Donald Trump has attacked US district judge Ana Reyes over her interventions to slow his plan to ‘restore’ the East Potomac golf course in Washington DC.

Citing environmental and historic preservation concerns, Reyes had ruled earlier this year that the federal government must give notice before any substantive construction work on the East Potomac golf course could proceed, and last week issued an order halting the removal of trees at the site, which she called “inexcusable”.

“The United States Department of Interior wants to take a terrible and very unsafe golf course, and make it into a great, safe, and prestigious golf course. They have an absolute right to do so. It’s as simple as that! The judge on the case is a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane? The tapes have been blocked from usage by the judge.

“The random golfer bringing the ridiculous lawsuit has ZERO STANDING! The experts at “Interior” are allowed to do this First Class renovation “as of right.” They do not need an approval. Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY! The finished product will be World Class, and bring income and great prestige back to D.C. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DJT.”
Rubio denies US paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine
Marco Rubio, the secretary of state denied on Monday that the United States had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contradicting Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Rubio, speaking to reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday morning, said intelligence was in fact never interrupted in the first place.
“I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause.
“What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused on.”
Zelenskyy thanked Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing, but maintained US sabotaged Starlink internet access

Volodymyr Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration on Sunday for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access so that Donald Trump could send a “message” in his ongoing feud with the Ukrainian president.
In an interview on NBC, Zelenskyy said the US had “unblocked” intelligence on impending Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have pounded the country’s energy infrastructure as winter draws in.

“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press. “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”

Zelenskyy also said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starlink terminals worked in Ukraine, hampering drone operations on the frontlines as well as some air defence missions.
“It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed,” he said. “And technically, SpaceX did it.”
Vice-president JD Vance expected to hold rally in North Carolina
The US vice-president JD Vance is expected to hold rally in North Carolina on Monday as the Trump administration continues ramping up rallies to support candidates in the 2026 midterm elections.

Vance’s visit comes as Republicans look to gain ground in North Carolina’s Senate race, as well as in two key US House races. Republican Michael Whatley, whom Trump endorsed, is running against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper for the seat vacated by Republican US Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection.

Henderson, in the heart of the state’s 11th congressional district, and Greenville, just outside the 1st congressional district are where voters strongly supported Trump in 2024 but now, as voters face rising gas and grocery prices, are in play. Democratic victories there could help them flip control of Congress.
US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
Andrew Roth

Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence in order to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.

Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at around 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a successive strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.

“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.

“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Donald Trump will attend a campaign rally in Kansas later today, where incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall is in an unexpectedly close race with Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Marshall’s medical billing scandal is threatening to erode his support, though he is still favored to win.
Hamilton, the founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, won in a crowded Democratic primary earlier this year.

Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary. His campaign announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party’s primary.
Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close.

articles.headline: Crusader Kings 3's merchant republics expansion, Silk and Silver, will release during the very quiet time of mid-November 2026
keyFacts: Paradox announced that the Crusader Kings 3 expansion Silk and Silver will release on November 17th.
The DLC focuses on merchant republics, allowing players to build trading companies, influence laws, and rule as a Doge.
Paradox stated that the expansion will not include naval warfare due to development constraints and balancing.
body: The second big expansion coming to Crusader Kings 3 this year finally has a proper release date. Silk and Silver, the gold-clinking sibling of recently released Church-centric DLC By God Alone, will arrive on November 17th. Just a couple of days before that which shall not be named, but has resulted in a lot of studios opting to give mid-November a wide berth release-wise.

Part of CK3's fifth chapter of DLC, Silk and Silver does for merchant republics like Venice what By God Alone did for realms ruled by Popes and priests. This time, the route to power is starting a successful trading company and building up your patrician family to the point of being able to rule as a palm-greasing Doge.

You'll be able to influence what areas your republic specialises in, such as naval trade, bread and circuses populism, or establishing a deep class of nobles to send out across Europe in the hopes of currying favour. In terms of laws and customs, there's a constitution you can try to shape to maximise your own ends or deliver good for the people. In terms of foreign policy, it'll be up to you which trade routes to pursue control of and whether you're after a monopoly or are happy to work with other republics for mutual benefit in trade leagues.

Sadly, it isn't set to introduce naval warfare to CK3 despite its maritime trading focus. "We know this is a topic people care about and relate to the republics strongly," Paradox wrote in deep dive about Silk and Silver earlier this year. "but between a whole lot of balancing and a whole lot of new systems that we are adding to the game, we chose not to spend time and energy on trying to pack in another large feature that we would not be able to give it enough love and time to do well."

All in all, I'm not sure the marchant republics will have as much meme potential as playable Popes have for CK3, even in cases that don't see the game glitch out and let you marry three ladies you shouldn't before having divorce them all in a single day. Then again, being a medieval business tycoon could allow for plenty of other hijnks and tomfoolery that'll make the decades roll by in funny fashion. Plus, it's something else to stop us PC folks being starved of new releases as the console lot crack into, well, you know.

articles.headline: Uber dodges £340M cabbie lawsuit after drivers miss legal deadline
keyFacts: A High Court judge dismissed a £340 million lawsuit against Uber by London black cab drivers and hire companies because the claims were filed past the six-year legal deadline, according to the ruling.
The claimants had accused Uber of misleading Transport for London to secure its operating license, but the court did not decide whether the allegations of fraud were true.
While the ruling is a victory for Uber, minicab drivers in London are now opposing new plans to introduce robotaxis to the capital.
body: Uber has dodged a £340 million lawsuit brought by thousands of London black cab drivers after a High Court judge ruled that they'd left it too late to sue. Monday's ruling kills off two claims involving around 13,000 cabbies and former private hire companies Kabbee and Iride, which accused Uber of misleading Transport for London (TfL) to secure its operating license. The cabbies wanted nearly £200 million in compensation for lost earnings, while Kabbee and Iride sought another £140 million. But the court never got as far as deciding whether Uber had done anything wrong. The claims were filed in May and June 2024, but Mr Justice Simon Birt ruled they were too late under the six-year time limit. The cabbies insisted that they hadn't had enough evidence to allege fraud until June 2018, but the judge wasn't buying it. According to the judgment, seen by The Register, three cabbies had already filed their own claims against Uber in September 2017. Litigation funder Harbour approached law firm Mishcon de Reya about a larger lawsuit that December, and by February 2018, the Licensed Taxi Drivers' Association was telling members about the planned action. The dispute dates back to Uber's arrival in London in 2012. The claimants alleged that the company deliberately misled TfL about how its booking system worked, allowing it to operate when it shouldn't have been permitted to do so. Uber has some history here. In a separate licensing appeal in 2018, the company admitted that it gave TfL and the High Court false information about how bookings were accepted through its app. The magistrate stopped short of finding dishonesty, however, and granted Uber a new 15-month license. The judgment also revisits Greyball, Uber's software for identifying suspected regulators, and Ripley, a tool used to remotely lock computers during regulatory visits. Uber maintained that Ripley hadn't been used that way in the UK. The cabbies insisted that they needed information from the June 2018 licensing appeal to support their fraud allegations. Justice Birt disagreed, finding that enough information had been available earlier to bring a claim. Things then went quiet. Mishcon sent Uber a letter before action in July 2019, but Harbour pulled its funding that November. The claimants didn't write to Uber again about the potential lawsuit for another four and a half years, according to the judgment, and by the time proceedings began in 2024, the deadline had passed. The ruling is a victory for Uber, but doesn't clear it of the alleged fraud. The judge dismissed the claims because they were filed too late, without deciding whether the allegations, which Uber denies, were true. Neither Uber nor RGL Management, the company representing the cabbies, responded to The Register’s questions. London's taxi wars are far from over. Minicab Drivers are now pushing back against plans to bring robotaxis to the capital, warning that driverless cars could put thousands of jobs at risk. Uber is working with British autonomous driving startup Wayve on driverless technology. Having spent years battling London's cabbies for passengers, it's now helping develop cars that won't need drivers at all. ®

articles.headline: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
keyFacts: Character.AI declared bankruptcy as part of a deal allowing Disney to hire most of its staff and acquire its technology.
Court filings indicate the bankruptcy allows Character.AI to handle ongoing lawsuits while Disney avoids those legal liabilities.
This arrangement is described as a reverse acquihire, which lets buyers obtain talent and technology without traditional merger requirements.
body: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.

In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.

The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.

Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.

articles.headline: Rubio says Ukraine attacked ships carrying US-owned oil, demands Zelensky bring ‘an end to this war’
keyFacts: Rubio stated that Ukrainian strikes hit energy vessels in the Black Sea carrying oil belonging to American companies.
Rubio denied that the Trump administration has paused intelligence-sharing with Kyiv regarding impending Russian missile attacks.
Rubio asserted that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should focus on bringing an end to the war.
body: “We have seen strikes on energy vessels in the Black Sea. And there’s been complaints, a lot, because we have American companies calling us and saying, ‘Hey, that was our oil on that ship that was hit by Ukraine,'” Rubio told Breitbart in an interview released Sunday.

“Now, I don’t believe Ukraine intentionally targeted them, but those ships got hit. And we already have a world that is facing an energy crisis,” he added. “We don’t need any exacerbating situations. And there’s been frustration that despite these asks, that has happened.”
Rubio also insisted Monday that the Trump administration has not paused intelligence-sharing meant to warn Kyiv of impending Russian ballistic missile attacks.

“I don’t know where he’s getting these things from or why he’s saying these things to the press,” Rubio told reporters in Uzbekistan in response to Zelensky’s latest complaint. “There’s been no pause. Zelensky should be focused on bringing an end to this war.”

Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have risen since President Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement that the US would import hundreds of thousands of gallons of diesel fuel in a bid to relieve prices at the pump.

During a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin that same day, the Kremlin tyrant suggested that he, Trump, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping sit down and come up with a way to end the brutal war, the Wall Street Journal reported Monday.

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump posted on Truth Social Sunday amid bipartisan criticism of his handling of the war in Ukraine. “Great progress is being made.”

“Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way,” he added. “Zelensky is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.”

Meanwhile, Ukraine has insisted that its access to a military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite system, known as Starshield, was throttled in systems moving faster than 100 miles per hour last week — preventing its air defenses from responding to Russian-launched, Iranian-made Shahed drones.
Zelensky stressed over the weekend that US intelligence about Russian attcks isn’t replaceable.

“We have dozens of countries who help,” he told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday. “But only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it.”
With the Russian invasion of Ukraine set to mark its fifth anniversary in February of next year, Rubio said Monday that “no one’s winning that war.”

“This war is honestly about one part of Ukraine called Donetsk. The Russians occupy all but about 11% of that area in that province, Donetsk, or in that region of Donetsk,” Rubio told Breitbart. “The Ukrainians have a defensive line that they’ve embedded themselves in. They argue, and military strategists say is true, that it is the last defensible line. That if they give that up, there is nothing to defend Kyiv.”

“The Russians have not been able to advance in the battlefield and take that region … The United States remains willing, able, and prepared to play a mediating role if the opportunity presents itself to end this war through a negotiated settlement, which is how we think this war will ultimately end.”

articles.headline: Dramatic images show violent unrest sweeping across France
keyFacts: Widespread violence and looting erupted across France over the weekend, resulting in nearly 2,400 arrests and almost 1,000 injured emergency workers, the French Interior Ministry said.
Demonstrators clashed with police, set fire to municipal buildings including a historic town hall in Limoges, and smashed windows during protests over living costs and school conditions.
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed on Sunday to take legal action and hold accountable those responsible for the violence.
body: Widespread violence erupted across France over the weekend, as rioters and looters ransacked storefronts, clashed with police and set fire to municipal buildings.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured, the French Interior Ministry said, after some of the worst unrest the country has seen in years.

In cities across the country, demonstrators set fire to newsstands and smashed windows. The violence followed weeks of largely peaceful protests over the cost of living and school conditions that expanded with an attempt to revive the “yellow vest” movement Saturday.
In Limoges, a town in central France, dramatic scenes emerged overnight Saturday as rioters broke into the historic town hall and set it ablaze.
Aerial images the following morning revealed the smoldering remains of the 19th century building, which had survived two world wars, capping one of the most violent days in France’s recent history.
Across the country in Lyon, southeastern France, an elderly man wearing a gas mask fled from tear gas at the Place des Terreaux on Saturday.
Crowds massed along the narrow streets of Paris throughout the weekend as masked demonstrators set up burning barricades near Place de la Republique, a major intersection through the city.
Striking scenes of disorder emerged from the French capital, including the monument at Place de la Republique where masked demonstrators burned flares and waved flags on Saturday.
Nearby, a man with a crucifix bearing the message “Love will triumph” rested near a burning vehicle in central Paris.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed legal action against those responsible for the violence. “Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” he said.

A High Court judge ruled that the lawsuits were filed too late because the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.
RGL Management, which represented the claimants, stated it was very disappointed and was considering its legal options.
body: - Published
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about Â£340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.
The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.
But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.
Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.

articles.headline: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
keyFacts: Apple updated its developer guidelines to ban AI-generated offensive content and apps that use bait-and-switch tactics to hide nudify features during the review process.
Apple stated that it will remove any apps that add unapproved features after submission, and reinforced bans on human trafficking and child exploitation.
San Francisco ordered Apple and Google in July to delete nudification apps, following reports that the tech giants hosted multiple apps of this type.
body: Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.

The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.

“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users, and removed 193,000 developer accounts on account of fraud and abuse.

In July, San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

articles.headline: NBA Arenas Get a Massive AT&T Network Upgrade to Boost Fan Experiences
keyFacts: The NBA, WNBA, and AT&T are installing the fourth generation of their High Speed Arena Network infrastructure starting with the 2026-27 season.
The network upgrade includes over 68,000 miles of AT&T fiber and provides four times the bandwidth of the existing infrastructure across 30 venues.
The NBA, WNBA, and AT&T also extended their marketing agreement, with AT&T continuing to serve as the leagues' Official Connectivity Partner.
body: The days of simply sitting in front of a TV and watching a pro basketball game are long gone. Now your game experience probably includes following real-time stats and player spotlights on your phone, along with keeping an eye on a different game on a tablet or laptop nearby whose outcome could move your favorite team up or down in the rankings.

That requires an enormous and ever-growing amount of data and coordination. To keep up with that demand and to anticipate tomorrow’s needs, the National Basketball Association, Women’s National Basketball Association and AT&T are installing the fourth generation of their High Speed Arena Network infrastructure starting with the 2026-27 season,

“It’s more, more, more,” said Ken DeGennaro, executive vice president of media operations and technology at the NBA, explaining the demands the organization sees every time two teams tip-off. “More video angles, higher density video angles, video content, higher frame video, higher quality video, all of that.”
More from CNET

The fourth-gen network is being installed in all 30 venues where the NBA operates, starting with the Intuit Dome in Inglewood, California, Barclays Center in New York City, United Center in Chicago, American Airlines Center in Dallas, State Farm Arena in Atlanta and Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The official launch of the updated HSAN will happen in July 2027.
A full-court press of live data
The network upgrade will include more than 68,000 miles of AT&T fiber and all new networking equipment at the venues. That will provide four times the bandwidth as the existing infrastructure.

DeGennaro said an average game uses about 118 streams of high-quality, low-latency data. “The majority of the video content comes back as uncompressed video at about 250 megabits per second per stream, so it’s quite a bit of throughput bandwidth on the network,” he said.

That includes the live broadcast video, in-arena content, studio programming by the league and regional sports networks, mobile viewing content and virtual signage. Those streams are also split out for redundancy and resiliency.
“We’ve gone from point-to-point networks to a full network that allows for greater reliability and scalability across all of our ingest and distribution channels,” DeGennaro said.

The work to upgrade the venues goes beyond installing new server racks and fresh fiber, though those are essential components. In some locations, that means breaking ground to bring fiber-filled conduit into the venue from different directions so it doesn’t all pass through a single potential failure point.

Joe Drygas, vice president of global enterprise solutions at AT&T Business, pointed to the increased capacity and the diverse architecture of data centers that can immediately pick up the slack if needed. AT&T has a dedicated engineering unit running network telemetry 24/7, predictive capacity modeling and automated traffic rerouting around bottlenecks.

“Ultimately, what you can’t have is any kind of disruption during games,” Drygas said, especially when multiple games are happening simultaneously. “Once the season starts across all these teams, it’s go time.”

Although the HSAN is focused on getting the NBA’s content out to the world, Drygas said AT&T is also focused on the overall network experience for fans, too, including the company’s Turbo Live service for prioritizing mobile data in highly congested environments like games and concerts.

“[In the venue] one of the first things people do is have their phones out. They’re taking videos, they’re live streaming, a lot of [data] is uploading out from the venue,” said Drygas. “So it’s really changed the way we architect these networks, so [the NBA] absolutely could leverage that and take advantage of other uses.”
Both Drygas and DeGennaro reiterated that they’re also looking ahead to additional venues that will need to be outfitted, both in the US and across the globe, as professional basketball expands.

“When we built out our first version of the high-speed arena network, we would have never envisioned where we are today,” said DeGennaro. He said the collaboration between the NBA and AT&T lets them keep up with fan demand.
NBA, WNBA and AT&T also extend their marketing agreement

In addition to the fourth-generation HSAN announcement, AT&T, the NBA and the WNBA extended their marketing partnership, with AT&T serving as the leagues’ Official Connectivity Partner. That extends to the NBA G League, USA Basketball and NBA Take-Two Media.

“The WNBA’s growth has been incredible to be a part of, and it takes partners who are committed to investing in the game and its future,” said A’ja Wilson, three-time WNBA Champion, five-time Kia WNBA MVP and Las Vegas Aces center, in a statement. “AT&T has consistently shown up for our league, our players and our fans.”

articles.headline: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
keyFacts: Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured after being struck by a car outside her office.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese stated that the collision was a deliberate act and not an accident.
Police arrested a 43-year-old driver at the scene and recovered a knife from the vehicle.
body: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'

MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.
Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.
Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.
"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.
"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.
Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.
Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.

articles.headline: Trump is coming for your credit card rewards. That’s good.
keyFacts: President Donald Trump has escalated his support for the Credit Card Competition Act to reduce retailer swipe fees.
Wall Street banks warned policymakers that lowering swipe fees could eliminate credit card cash rewards and travel points.
Research indicates that current swipe fees redistribute money from lower-income cash shoppers to wealthier reward-earning cardholders.
body: President Donald Trump points after addressing attendees on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center on September 9, 2026 in Dallas. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Wall Street is sending the public a dire warning: President Donald Trump has become a threat to the very foundation of American freedom — your frequent flier miles.
Okay, America’s big banks haven’t been using rhetoric quite that grandiose. But they are accusing Trump of imperiling Americans’ credit card rewards.

The feud between Wall Street and the White House centers on the Credit Card Competition Act (CCCA). Long stalled in Congress, that legislation aims to drive down the “swipe fees” that merchants pay to banks when customers use credit cards. In theory, if those fees fall, retailers might pass on some of the savings to consumers, in the form of lower prices.

Trump first endorsed the bill in January . But he’s ramped up his advocacy for it recently, amid a broader ( belated ) push to address voters’ affordability concerns ahead of November’s midterms. Last week, the White House urged Congress to “ put Main Street over Wall Street ” by enacting the law. On Monday, Trump praised Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall for “working tirelessly to pass the Credit Card Competition Act, in order to stop the out of control Swipe Fee ripoff!”

The financial industry is used to taking fire from Trump right before Election Day, then receiving favorable treatment from him thereafter. But in this case, Trump’s threat is not entirely idle. Large retailers are lobbying hard to get the Credit Card Competition Act passed during December’s lame-duck congressional session. Banks have responded by issuing a “code red,” in the words of the Wall Street Journal . In recent days, their lobbyists have warned policymakers that, if swipe fees fall, credit cardholders’ cash rewards and travel points will go down with them.

In truth, the consequences of the Credit Card Competition Act are uncertain. But if the banks’ big-picture story is right — and the law cuts both swipe fees and credit card rewards — that would probably benefit the average American.
Poor people pay for your travel points
To see why, we need to first examine how the credit card system currently works — and whom it does and doesn’t benefit.

Whenever you use a credit card to purchase a banana from Aldi, or volleyball from Dick’s, or an adult-sized Grape Fanta Can Halloween costume from Party City, the retailer must pay a fee to the bank that issued your card. The bank then uses that revenue to fund your rewards.

Critically, merchants don’t just eat the costs of swipe fees. Rather, they pass on part of the expense to consumers, in the form of higher prices. Some businesses concentrate these price hikes on card users (for example, barbershops often charge less if you pay with cash). But most retailers charge every customer the same price , regardless of their payment method.

For this reason, shoppers who pay with cash or debit effectively subsidize those who pay with cards: The former face higher prices than they would in a world without credit cards, yet they receive no “cash back” or travel points in recompense.
This arrangement seems unfair on its face. But it is especially troubling when one considers class disparities in the use of credit cards and receipt of rewards.

As a general rule, the higher a person’s income, the more they use credit cards. In 2024, US households who earned less than $25,000 a year put just 17 percent of their payments on credit cards; among households earning more than $150,000, that figure was 51 percent, according to Federal Reserve data.
What’s more, the rich are also more likely to qualify for premium cards that charge merchants exceptionally high fees, in order to fund extraordinarily lavish benefits.

As a result of all this, swipe fees effectively redistribute money from poor and working-class people to affluent and wealthy ones. According to a 2026 working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research, the credit card system takes, on average, $88 a year from households with annual incomes below $150,000, while delivering an average yearly benefit of $390 to households with incomes above that threshold.

American swipe fees are too damn high

To be sure, this does not mean that lower-income Americans would be better off in a world where credit cards didn’t exist. Such cards serve a variety of valuable economic purposes, from helping households weather unexpected expenses and irregular incomes to facilitating online commerce. And maintaining a credit card system costs money: Banks need to finance the loans they extend, while payment networks must maintain vast computer systems to process transactions and detect fraud.
Yet America’s credit card system is needlessly expensive. Our nation’s merchants — and thus, consumers — pay far higher swipe fees than their counterparts in other rich countries.

To take one illustrative example: When an American buys $100 worth of groceries using a standard Visa card , the supermarket must pay the issuing bank a minimum of $1.23. Some disfavored stores must pay as much as $1.57 on such a purchase. If a customer uses a premium “Visa Infinite” card, meanwhile, the grocer’s fee can run as high as $2.07.
By contrast, in Canada, a grocery purchase worth $100 US dollars would incur a fee worth 95 cents if the customer used a standard Visa card.
In Australia and the European Union , meanwhile, government regulations would cap that fee at 30 cents (or .3 percent), no matter what kind of card was used.

Suffice to say, Australia and the EU manage to sustain functional credit card systems, despite charging merchants a tiny fraction of the swipe fees absorbed by US businesses. And although retailers have pocketed some of these savings, research suggests that fee caps have also lowered consumer prices.

This affordability gain does come at a cost; American cardholders do tend to reap higher rewards than Australian or European ones. But this is not a good trade from the standpoint of economic justice; few think it is fair to take money from the poor to give to the rich.
The Credit Card Competition Act might not work

All this said, whether the Credit Card Competition Act would actually yield those outcomes is uncertain. The bill does not directly regulate swipe fees. Instead, as the name suggests, it aims to give credit card companies greater competition.

Today, each time you buy an adult-size Grape Fanta Can Halloween costume with a Visa, Party City is required to process your purchase using Visa’s network. Which means it needs to pay whatever swipe fee Visa decrees. The store can protest an exorbitant rate by refusing to accept Visa cards. But this would send a large number of customers into the hands of Spirit Halloween . So its leverage is limited.

Under the CCCA, however, Party City would be able to accept Visa on a transaction — without necessarily using Visa to process the payment. Instead, the bank that issued the customer’s Visa would need to provide Party City with at least one alternative payment processor — a different network that has no relationship with Visa and which might offer lower fees.
The law’s authors hope — and the banking industry fears — that this mandatory competition will force down swipe fees. But it’s not clear how much of a difference the CCCA would actually make.

After all, under the law, banks would still get to choose the alternative payment network available to retailers when their customers pay with Visa (or Mastercard, or American Express, etc.). Party City would no longer need to pony up whatever Visa asks when a shopper pays with a Visa-Bank of America card. But if the store did decline to use Visa’s network, it would then need to partner with Bank of America’s hand-selected alternative. And since banks benefit from high swipe fees, BofA would have an incentive to pick an expensive backup option.

Nevertheless, the banks and retailers both seem to believe that the CCCA will sharply reduce swipe fees. If they’re right, then Congress shouldn’t vote down the bill, merely to protect affluent Americans’ travel points.

It doubtlessly feels nice to receive a free flight or hotel stay, as a reward for spending a lot of money on yourself. But the poor probably should not have to pay higher prices, just so the affluent can enjoy such satisfactions.
